steps.premise: An ensemble that knows the room's equipment in advance can set up faster.
steps.action: Post a dated inventory next to the booking form.
steps.consequence: Players can decide which equipment they need to bring.
steps.quote: A quartet can set up much faster if it knows what is already in the room. Put a dated equipment list beside the booking form so players can decide what to bring.

steps.premise: Putting away cases and stands can run into the next booking.
steps.action: Allow packing time between rehearsal slots.
steps.consequence: A slow departure costs the next group less rehearsal time.
steps.quote: Leave a gap between bookings for packing cases and folding stands. A slow pack-up then takes less time out of the next group's rehearsal.

steps.premise: Cello endpins slip on the polished floor.
steps.action: Store endpin stops near the chairs.
steps.consequence: Cellists can keep their instruments in place while playing.
steps.quote: A cello endpin slides on the polished floor. Keep a few endpin stops with the chairs so cellists can play without chasing their instruments forward.

steps.premise: Some musicians arrive after rehearsal starts.
steps.action: Include the entry code in the booking message.
steps.consequence: Latecomers can let themselves in while the ensemble continues playing.
steps.quote: Some players arrive after everyone else has begun. Giving them the door code in the booking message saves the ensemble from stopping mid-piece to let them in.

steps.premise: Afternoon sunlight shines across the score on the piano.
steps.action: Fit a blind to the window admitting the light.
steps.consequence: The pianist can read the music with the piano in its usual place.
steps.quote: The afternoon sun falls straight across the piano score. A blind on that window lets the pianist read the page without having to move the instrument.

steps.premise: Musicians use pencils to mark bowings during rehearsal.
steps.action: Give every stand a clip or groove for a pencil.
steps.consequence: Each player has a pencil within reach.
steps.quote: Put a pencil groove or clip on each music stand. Players mark bowings as they rehearse, and a pencil that stays on the stand is always within reach.

steps.premise: Someone reports a chair with a loose leg.
steps.action: Mark the chair and remove it from the rehearsal floor immediately.
steps.consequence: The next player avoids sitting on the unstable chair.
steps.quote: Flag a wobbly chair and take it off the floor as soon as someone reports it. Otherwise the next player is likely to discover the loose leg by sitting on it.

steps.premise: Drums can overpower quieter instruments in a small room.
steps.action: Provide practice pads for the drum kit.
steps.consequence: Players can hear the softer parts as they rehearse together.
steps.quote: A drum kit can drown a flute in a small room. Stock a set of practice pads so mixed groups can hear the quieter parts while they work through a passage.

steps.premise: Players arriving with wheeled cases may find steps at the main entrance.
steps.action: Mark the level entrance on the map sent with a booking.
steps.consequence: Players can find the accessible door without searching the block.
steps.quote: Show the accessible entrance on the booking map. The front steps can leave a player with a wheeled case searching the block for the level doorway.

steps.premise: Brass musicians need to drain water from their instruments.
steps.action: Supply absorbent mats that can be washed.
steps.consequence: The next group finds the floor free of water spots.
steps.quote: Brass players need somewhere to empty water from their instruments. Washable absorbent mats keep those spots off the floor for the following group.

steps.premise: A last-minute cancellation may leave too little time to advertise the slot.
steps.action: Keep a list of local ensembles that volunteer for short-notice bookings.
steps.consequence: Another group can use the canceled rehearsal time.
steps.quote: A rehearsal cancellation sometimes comes too late to advertise. An opt-in list of local groups willing to take short-notice slots would put those empty hours to use.

steps.premise: Loose pages from different arrangements get mixed and take time to sort.
steps.action: File spare scores upright in folders marked for each ensemble.
steps.consequence: Groups can begin playing without sorting out the pages first.
steps.quote: Store spare scores upright in folders labeled by ensemble. Loose sheets from different arrangements otherwise end up together, taking time to sort before the first piece.

steps.premise: Groups may change the seating during their booking.
steps.action: Post a photograph of the usual chair arrangement inside the door.
steps.consequence: Groups can restore the room after trying another layout.
steps.quote: Photograph the standard chair layout and post it inside the door. Groups can try a different seating arrangement and still put the room back as they found it.

steps.premise: The room becomes stuffy with a dozen musicians playing.
steps.action: Open the windows during the tea break.
steps.consequence: Players return to fresher air after the break.
steps.quote: The room gets stuffy once a dozen people are playing. Opening the windows during the tea break gives everyone fresher air when rehearsal resumes.

steps.premise: Large instrument cases on the floor obstruct players coming in late.
steps.action: Put shelves for cases against a wall away from the door.
steps.consequence: Arriving players have room to reach their seats.
steps.quote: Put case shelves along a wall away from the doorway. Large instrument cases spread across the floor leave very little room for a late arrival to reach a seat.

steps.premise: The conductor needs to leave time for the final piece.
steps.action: Provide a clock the conductor can see from their spot.
steps.consequence: The conductor can pace rehearsal without pausing to check a phone.
steps.quote: A clock visible from the conductor's spot makes it easier to leave time for the last piece without breaking off to check a phone.

steps.premise: Musicians often move around and can trip over exposed speaker cables.
steps.action: Route each powered speaker cable along a wall beneath a cable cover.
steps.consequence: A passing musician is less likely to catch a foot on a lead.
steps.quote: Run each powered speaker's lead along the wall under a cable cover. Players frequently change places, and an exposed lead can catch a foot in passing.

steps.premise: A group may change individual mixer channels during its booking.
steps.action: Photograph the normal mixer settings.
steps.consequence: The next ensemble can quickly find a starting setup.
steps.quote: A photo of the mixer's usual settings gives the next ensemble a quick starting point after a group has turned individual channels up or down.

steps.premise: Groups planning recordings may want a freshly tuned piano.
steps.action: Enter the piano tuner's visit on the shared calendar.
steps.consequence: Groups can book a recording shortly after the tuning.
steps.quote: Leave the piano tuner's visit on the shared calendar. Ensembles scheduling a recording can pick a date when the instrument will have just been tuned.

steps.premise: A visitor may feel uncomfortable being recorded.
steps.action: Ask visitors about recording before the rehearsal take starts.
steps.consequence: Visitors have a chance to voice concerns before recording begins.
steps.quote: Ask visitors before recording a rehearsal. Someone who is uncomfortable being recorded then has time to speak up before a take begins.
